items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: He was like a father. When I first joined the band I was 19 and he just took a liking to me and he introduced me to Ellington, James P. Johnson, Art Tatum, Louis Armstrong, oh my goodness.

ctx.x: How do you feel about that? How did that effect the music? Do you think it was a —

Oh, it had its toll on jazz because there are no more big bands, there are I think only the Count Basie Band and the Duke Ellington Band, but it’s not like the leader was there, like if you cut the head of a snake off, the tail dies, and the head of the snake was like the band leader, like Count Basie. The big bands were so popular in those days, until, and they, most of the musicians in those days demanded respect because they were an artist. And they were all individualists. Everybody had a sound of their own. They could be identified on the record like if Billie Holiday would sing on the record you’d know it’s nobody but Billie Holiday. items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: No, I didn’t get to meet him... Duke Ellington’s show used to come there from the Cotton Club... I used to stand on the outside of the fence, there, and listen to Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington...

ctx.x: Did you get to meet him at that time?

No, I didn’t get to meet him because they hurried me from backstage, I wasn’t supposed to be there anyway, because this was an all-white theater but black performers used to perform there. Like, they used to have the Cotton Club Revue there downtown, and we weren’t even allowed in the balcony. The Cab Calloway show used to come there from the Cotton Club. Duke Ellington’s show used to come there from the Cotton Club. Don Redman and his band used to come to that theater, the Connie’s Inn Revue. But if they didn’t…
No, I meant about the reading and everything? You could --

Yeah. Yeah, yeah, but it still wasn't -- you know, it took a lot of rehearsals to get what you wanted to get. And they had one guy, Chappie Willett, he used to write such hard arrangements it would take so long to get these players together. And musicians could read in those days, because Don Redman had a fantastic band. So did Duke. So did Jimmy Lunceford. So did Fletcher, Fletcher had a good band and he always wrote in the hard keys. That's why all the good musicians came out of Fletcher's band, you know.

In fact, all the musicians in those days were good musicians. They knew how to read. [But Basie's band was based on head arrangements because everybody took solos in Basie's band. Basie's band wasn't an ensemble band. It was noted for soloists, you know. Everybody was a fantastic soloist.]
